Forest Research is the Research Agency of the Forestry Commission and is the leading UK organisation engaged in forestry and tree related research.

The Agency aims to support and enhance forestry and its role in sustainable development by providing innovative, high quality scientific research, data, technical support and consultancy services.

### Introduction

This chapter contains information about world forestry, presenting global figures by region alongside data for the UK and the EU. Topics covered include woodland area, carbon stocks, wood removals, production, and apparent consumption of wood products and international trade in forest products.

The data is produced by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO). All of the statistics presented in this chapter have been previously released by the FAO. Further information on revisions, data sources, and methodology used to compile the figures is provided in Chapter 10: Sources and Methodology.

Data for the European Union (EU) relate to all 27 current EU members, excluding the UK, for all the years shown. Data for Europe cover 26 of the EU members (excluding Cyprus), Russia, and a number of other European countries, including Norway, Switzerland, Serbia, and Ukraine. Cyprus is included in the EU total, but is part of FAO’s Asia region and is thus not included in the Europe total.

These figures are outside the scope of Accredited Official Statistics. For further information see Chapter 10: Sources and Methodology.

Please refer to Glossary - Forest Research for a glossary of terms used in this release.

Figures in tables have been independently rounded, so may not add to the totals shown. Percentage changes quoted in this release are based on unrounded figures.

### Key findings

The main findings are:

• At around 14% forest cover in 2025, the UK is one of the least densely forested countries in Europe. This compares with 47% for Europe as a whole and 32% worldwide. 

• The global forest area reduced by around 7.7 million hectares (0.1%) per year between 2020 and 2025.

• Carbon stocks in forest living biomass have increased in Europe, North & Central America, and Asia between 1990 and 2025 and have shown an overall increase at a global level over this period. 
• Around 3.9 billion cubic metres underbark of wood was removed from global forests in 2024, of which around one-half (50%) was used as industrial roundwood (for use by wood processors) and the remainder as woodfuel. 
• Global production of wood products in 2024 totalled 445 million cubic metres of sawnwood, 393 million cubic metres of wood-based panels, and 423 million tonnes of paper and paperboard. 

• Europe consumed 25% of all sawnwood, 20% of the world’s wood-based panels and 20% of all paper and paperboard in 2024.

• The UK was the third largest net importer (imports less exports) of forest products in 2024, with net imports of US $8.1 billion. The largest net importer was China, with net imports of US $26.9 billion. 

### 9.1 Forest cover: international

### comparisons

The FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment (FRA) is a collation of forest data undertaken by the United Nations FAO at the global level every five years.

The UK is one of the least densely forested countries in Europe, with around 14% of its total land area covered in forest in 2025 (Figure 9.1, Table 9.1). This compares with 47% for Europe as a whole and 32% worldwide.

### 9.2 Forest area by country

Figure 9.2 shows the countries with the largest forest areas. Around one-half (48%) of the total forest area of 4,127 million hectares in 2025 is located in four countries (Russia, Brazil, Canada, and the United States).

Figure 9.2 Forest area by country, World, 2025

Source: FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment (2025).

### 9.3 Annual changes in forest area

The global forest area has reduced from around 4,344 million hectares in 1990 to 4,127 million hectares in 2025. This represents a decrease of around 10.7 million hectares (0.2%) per year between 1990 and 2000; around 3.6 million hectares (0.1%) per year between 2000 and 2010; 3.6 million hectares (0.1%) between 2010 and 2020; and around 7.7 million hectares (0.1%) per year between 2020 and 2025 (Table 9.2).

The forest area has reduced in most regions since 1990, except for Europe and Asia (where areas have increased).

### 9.4 Forest carbon stocks

Overall, carbon stocks in forest living biomass have increased globally between 1990 and 2025 (Table 9.3), except for Africa and South America. This increase has been mainly driven by changes in Europe, North & Central America and Asia.

to 2025

Source: FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment (2025).

Notes:

1. A giga tonne is a thousand million tonnes (10 9 tonnes). 2. The Europe region covers 26 EU countries (excluding Cyprus), the UK, Russia and other countries, including Norway, Switzerland, Serbia and Ukraine.

In 2025, based on available FRA data reported by countries, Africa records the highest carbon stock globally at 223 tonnes per hectare, followed by North & Central America at 201 tonnes per hectare (Figure 9.4). Africa also has the largest share of carbon stored in soils (59%). The proportion of carbon in deadwood and litter is highest in North & Central America (22%), while South America has the greatest share of carbon stored in living biomass (67%) among the regions.

### 9.5 Wood removals

Around 3.9 billion cubic metres underbark of wood was removed from global forests in 2024, of which almost 2.0 billion cubic metres (50%) was for use as industrial roundwood (for use by wood processors) and the remainder was woodfuel (Table 9.4).

Europe accounted for almost one-third (30%) of all industrial roundwood removals in 2024. Globally, removals of industrial roundwood increased by 2% between 2023 and 2024.

Almost three-quarters (73%) of woodfuel removals in 2024 took place in Asia and Africa.
